extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral/intellectual history; scholars of ancient ethics
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length historical and philosophical analysis tracing how Roman and Greek influences, Stoicism, and later schools shaped the ideals of virtue and the moral character of the Roman world. Emphasis on the social, political, and intellectual causes of moral change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for simple, forcible, massive excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: “The kind of excellence that found most favour in Roman eyes was simple, forcible, massive, but coarse-grained. Subtilty of motives, refinements of feelings, delicacies of susceptibility, were rarely appreciated.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Roman ideal prizes simplicity, force, and large-scale moral traits over subtlety or delicate sensibilities. As an evaluative standard, works or characters are judged favorably if they exhibit straightforward, robust virtues rather than nuanced emotional refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic/military virtues: courage, frugality, honour, labour
rubrics_metrics.description: “Death being continually confronted, to meet it with courage was the chief test of virtue. The habits of men were unaffected, frugal, honourable, and laborious. A stern discipline... trained the will... to repress the passions, to endure suffering and opposition, to tend steadily and fearlessly towards an unpopular end. A sense of duty was very widely diffused, and a deep attachment to the interests of the city became the parent of many virtues.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral character by capacity for endurance, self-discipline, public duty, and readiness to face death. Anti-patterns: effeminacy, indulgence in luxury, failure to subordinate personal desire to civic duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoical ethics: reason reveals a law of nature; conformity independent of reward
rubrics_metrics.description: “It taught that our reason reveals to us a certain law of nature, and that a desire to conform to this law, irrespectively of all considerations of reward or punishment, of happiness or the reverse, is a possible and a sufficient motive of virtue.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral worth is measured by rational conformity to natural law rather than consequentialist calculations. Assessments should focus on motive (commitment to principle) and internal governance by reason rather than external incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic doctrine: will as sole principle of virtue; suppression of emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: “It taught... that the will, acting under the complete control of the reason, is the sole principle of virtue, and that all the emotional part of our being is of the nature of a disease. Its whole tendency was therefore to dignify and strengthen the will, and to degrade and suppress the desires.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral agents by strength and purity of will, control over passions, and subordination of desires. Consider as a shortcoming any ethical programme that places positive moral value on emotions or sympathy that weaken resolute will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic attitude to death and self-hastening
rubrics_metrics.description: “It taught... that man is capable of attaining an extremely high degree of moral excellence, that he has nothing to fear beyond the present life, that it is essential to the dignity and consistence of his character that he should regard death without dismay, and that he has a right to hasten it if he desires.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Stoic-standard moral evaluation regards fearlessness of death and equanimity about life’s end as marks of excellence; the controversial allowance of self-hastening is noted as consistent with dignity in this framework. Use caution when applying this standard in different cultural contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral systems must admit extensions and refinements of sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: “But it is not sufficient for a moral system to form a bulwark against vice, it must also be capable of admitting those extensions and refinements of moral sympathies which advancing civilisation produces...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging an ethical system, test its capacity to broaden conceptions of good as society advances (e.g., extending concern beyond clan/class to all classes and nations). A rigid system that cannot accommodate enlarging sympathies is judged defective for a developing civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from heroic to benevolent virtues; enlargement of moral sympathies
rubrics_metrics.description: “The changes... consisted of the increasing prominence of the benevolent or amiable, as distinguished from the heroic qualities, and of the enlargement of moral sympathies, which... came at last... to include all classes and all nations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral change by the relative prominence of benevolence/amiability versus heroic qualities. Indicators of progression: increased public esteem for mercy, pity, and philanthropy; legal/social inclusion across classes and nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek humanity and the sanctity of pity/mercy
rubrics_metrics.description: “The general humanity of the Greeks had always been incomparably greater than that of the Romans... The plays of Euripides had been... the first great revelation of the supreme beauty of the gentler virtues... There was an altar... dedicated to Pity... venerated... as the first great assertion among mankind of the supremo sanctity of Mercy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral ideals by the centrality of pity/mercy in literature and ritual: societies that institutionalize pity (civic reverence, literary celebration) are judged to have a more humanitarian moral standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cosmopolitanism: destruction of narrow national feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is evident, therefore, that the prevalence of Greek ideas in Rome would be in a two-fold way destructive of narrow national feelings... Alexander... created... a great centre both of commercial intercourse and of philosophical eclecticism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure moral development by openness to outsiders and the erosion of parochial duties. Philosophical eclecticism, universalist political projects, and practical interchange (commerce, travel) are markers of cosmopolitan moral orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/institutional conciliation as moral and social standard
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Roman method of conciliation was, first of all, the most ample toleration of the customs, religion, and municipal freedom of the conquered, and then their gradual admission to the privileges of the conqueror... by according to them the right of Roman citizenship...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate systems of governance by how they integrate conquered peoples: tolerance of local customs, municipal freedom, and incremental extension of rights (e.g., citizenship) indicate a morally stabilising and inclusive political ethic. Contrast with policies that preserve sharp class or national barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic doctrine of universal brotherhood and equality of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Stoic taught that virtue alone is a good, and that all other things are indifferent; and from this position he inferred that birth, rank, country, or wealth are the mere accidents of life... all men are fellow-members of a single body, united by participation in the same Divine Spirit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use universal brotherhood as an evaluative criterion: moral standing is independent of social status; institutions and opinions that treat persons as intrinsically equal in moral worth accord with this Stoic standard. Look for rhetorical/argumentative emphasis on common humanity in texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of Stoicism to an advancing, more tender civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: “But while Stoicism was quite capable of representing the widening movement, it was not equally capable of representing the softening movement of civilisation. Its condemnation of the affections... were unsuited for the mild manners and luxurious tastes of the age of the Antonines.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge ethical systems by fit with prevailing social temperament: a system that denigrates affections may be ill-suited where gentler virtues and emotional responsiveness gain prominence. Assessments should note adaptive flexibility or lack thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergence of gentler moral types (eclectics, peripatetics, Platonists)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A class of writers... formed or representing a moral character, less strong, less sublime, less capable of endurance and heroism... but far more tender and attractive... The virtues of force began to recede, and the gentler virtues to advance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral thought by its balance between force and tenderness. Newer moral voices are judged positively when they legitimate benevolent affections, consolation, and tenderness; however, they may be critiqued for diminished heroic stamina.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral pedagogy/style: Seneca's austere eloquence vs Plutarch's consoling tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative characterisation: Seneca's writings are 'austere, sometimes self-conscious... short sentences... granulated' and often 'rise to a majesty of eloquence'; Plutarch is 'more sustained, equable, and uniformly pleasing'—'the Montaigne of antiquity'—excelling in consolation and tenderness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing moral literature or moral instruction, consider rhetorical style and its moral effect: stern, trumpet-like exhortation (Seneca) suits formation of heroic endurance; gentle, consolatory discourse (Plutarch) suits consolation and cultivation of tender virtues. Choose style according to pedagogical aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Later Stoicism's growing religiosity and personal deity
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the first place, Stoicism became more essentially religious... the language of philosophers recognised with much greater clearness a distinct and personal Divinity. Every page of Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius is impregnated with the deepest religious feeling.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess developments in an ethical system by degree of religious incorporation: increasing emphasis on a personal Divinity marks a transformation that can broaden appeal to devotional audiences and reconcile Stoic practice with religious sentiment.
